paras: The attempted expulsion of Black residents from Ballinger, Texas, took place in May 1903, when whitecaps signing themselves the "Clearing Committee" posted notices ordering all Black people to leave the town by June 1 or "suffer the consequences." Mayor John Hoffer answered with a proclamation that Black residents should not be molested and deputized citizens to protect them, a response that most of the coverage emphasized. No violence was reported, and the coverage does not show whether any families left.

Ballinger was described in one later account as a town of somewhat more than a thousand inhabitants with a sizable Black population. A dispatch from the town said there were "a large number of negro families" there.

By May 20, written notices had been posted about the town, including on the post office, warning Black residents to leave. According to the Ballinger dispatch, the notices were signed "Clearing Committee" and set a deadline of June 1, after which those remaining would "suffer the consequences"; a Texas weekly described them as threats "to do bodily harm." Many of the Black families, the same dispatch said, intended to obey the notice "in order to avoid possible trouble."

By May 22, according to a Dallas special of that date, the mayor had issued a proclamation calling on "all peaceful and law-abiding citizens to act as a special police force to protect the negroes." The Shiner Gazette named the mayor as John Hoffer and said he had stated "very explicitly" that Black residents should not be molested and had appointed a number of prominent citizens as deputy marshals. That paper judged that the step would "probably prove effective" and that there was little fear of trouble.

A Spanish-language summary printed in San Juan in mid-June, however, said reports indicated that no Black person would remain in Ballinger well before the deadline. No report of arrests, of the notices' authors being identified, or of what happened on June 1 appears in the coverage.

The story reached the white press first as a one-line item in a Texas "News in Brief" column on May 20, which the Shreveport Caucasian printed on May 20 and again on May 21. The New York Sun carried the fuller Ballinger dispatch under the headline "Negroes Warned Out of Ballinger, Tex.," reporting the threat and the families' readiness to comply without comment. The Dallas special on the mayor's proclamation ran in Georgia as "Proclamation to Protect Negroes" and on the front page of the Montgomery Advertiser as "Negroes Warned to Leave."

In Kentucky, a syndicated digest line on the mayor calling out "the law-abiding whites" as special police appeared in Maysville, Stanford and Marion papers between May 25 and May 28. The Shiner Gazette's headline, "Whitecapping Tabooed," framed the episode around official disapproval of the whitecaps, while the Puerto Rico paper alone stressed the likely departure of the town's Black population. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

accounts.gist: Whitecaps signing 'Clearing Committee' posted notices ordering all negroes out by June 1 or suffer the consequences; many of the numerous Black families said they would obey.

accounts.label: Dallas special
accounts.gist: The mayor issued a proclamation calling on peaceful and law-abiding citizens to act as a special police force to protect the negroes.

accounts.label: Texas weekly (Shiner Gazette)
accounts.gist: The notices threatened bodily harm; Mayor John Hoffer forbade molestation and deputized prominent citizens, and little trouble was feared.

accounts.label: Puerto Rico summary
accounts.gist: Notices 'by order of the Cleaning Committee' set a June 1 deadline, and reports said no Black person would remain long before it.

framing.detail: The Sun headed its dispatch 'Negroes Warned Out of Ballinger, Tex.' and reported the threat and the families' compliance without comment.
Georgia, Alabama and Kentucky papers ran the Dallas special or a digest line on the mayor's 'special police force' ('Proclamation to Protect Negroes'; 'Negroes Warned to Leave').
The Shiner Gazette's headline 'Whitecapping Tabooed' and its approving note that the mayor's step 'will probably prove effective' sided with the official protection.
